title: Quadratic Equations — Chapter Summary
intro: A quadratic equation has the variable to the second power and no higher. Quadratics describe parabolic trajectories, area constraints, speed-and-current problems and many other situations. This chapter develops three solution methods (factorisation, completing the square, the quadratic formula), the discriminant test for the nature of roots, the link between roots and coefficients, and the translation of word problems into quadratics.

sections.heading: Standard Form and Roots
bullets: Standard form: ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.
If a = 0 the equation collapses to linear, not quadratic.
A root (zero) of the quadratic is a value of x making LHS = 0.
Geometrically, a root is an x-intercept of the parabola y = ax^2 + bx + c.
A quadratic has at most two real roots.
Verify by substitution: if p(α) = 0, then α is a root.

sections.heading: Solution by Factorisation
bullets: Re-arrange to standard form.
Factor the quadratic — usually by splitting the middle term.
Apply the zero-product property: if P · Q = 0 then P = 0 or Q = 0.
Set each factor to 0 and solve.
Limitation: only works for quadratics with rational factors.

sections.heading: Completing the Square
bullets: Always works (universal method).
Step 1: divide by a so leading coefficient is 1.
Step 2: move constant to the right side.
Step 3: add (b/(2a))^2 to both sides.
Step 4: write LHS as (x + b/(2a))^2.
Step 5: take square roots and solve for x.

sections.heading: The Quadratic Formula
bullets: Universal solver: x = (−b ± √(b^2 − 4ac)) / (2a).
Derived by completing the square on the general form.
Works for ALL quadratics, even those with irrational or complex roots.
When in doubt, use the formula.

sections.heading: Nature of Roots — The Discriminant
bullets: D = b^2 − 4ac.
D > 0 → two distinct real roots; parabola crosses x-axis at two points.
D = 0 → equal real roots (repeated); parabola is tangent to the x-axis.
D < 0 → no real roots; parabola does not cross the x-axis.
The discriminant tells us the NATURE of the roots without solving the equation.

sections.heading: Roots and Coefficients
bullets: If α and β are roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0, then:
Sum: α + β = −b/a.
Product: αβ = c/a.
Build a quadratic given roots α, β: x^2 − (α + β)x + αβ = 0.
Example: roots 3 and −5 → x^2 + 2x − 15 = 0.
These relations let us find one root given the other and the coefficients.

sections.heading: Word Problems
bullets: Routine: name the unknown x, translate sentence-by-sentence, write a quadratic, solve.
Always REJECT non-physical roots (negative ages, negative widths, negative speeds).
Common types: consecutive integers, area of rectangles, distance / speed / time, age problems, sum and reciprocal puzzles.
Verify the chosen root in the ORIGINAL words of the problem.

key_takeaways: Quadratic = degree 2; standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.
Three solution methods — factorisation, completing the square, quadratic formula.
Quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b^2 − 4ac))/(2a) works for ANY quadratic.
Discriminant tells you the nature of the roots before you solve.
In word problems, always reject non-physical roots.

glossary.definition: An equation of the form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.
A value of the variable that makes the LHS of the equation equal to 0.
ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with the right-hand side equal to 0.
One of the constants a, b, c that multiply the powers of x.
If P·Q = 0 then P = 0 or Q = 0; the basis of factorisation.
A technique that re-writes the quadratic as a perfect-square trinomial plus a constant.
D = b^2 − 4ac, which determines the nature of the roots.
Two different real numbers that satisfy the quadratic; occurs when D > 0.
A single value that is counted as both roots; occurs when D = 0.
The quadratic has no real solutions; occurs when D < 0.
α + β = −b/a for the equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
αβ = c/a for the equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
